title: Women workers and the Labour Codes
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Night work, maternity benefit, equal pay and where the gaps remain.
body:
Women are a large part of India's working population, but they are present in very different numbers in different kinds of work. They form a large share of scheme workers, domestic workers, home-based workers and agricultural labourers, and a smaller share of formal, salaried employees. That difference is the key to understanding what the new Labour Codes can and cannot do for women. This post sets out what the Codes provide, where the gaps are, and how BMS looks at the question.

## Why the Codes matter for women workers

When the four Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025, the Government's announcement gave a distinct place to women. It said that women may work night shifts and in all types of work, with their consent and with the required safety measures; that gender discrimination is prohibited and equal pay for equal work is mandated; that grievance committees must include women's representation; and that, for female employees, parents-in-law may be counted within the definition of family for benefits. These are statements by the Government of what the Codes are meant to do. How far they reach depends on rules, inspection and, above all, on whether a woman is in a workplace the law actually touches.

## Equal pay and non-discrimination

The Code on Wages prohibits discrimination on the ground of gender in wages and in recruitment for the same work or work of a similar nature. The Code explains what "similar" means: work that requires the same skill, effort, experience and responsibility. That definition is useful because many pay gaps are defended by claiming that a woman's job, though identical in practice, has a different name. The Code is also drafted to apply to all employees, and not only to workers in a list of scheduled industries, which widens its reach.

The practical test for a woman who suspects unequal pay is simple. She should compare what is paid for the same tasks, note the job descriptions, and keep her wage slips. Where the facts are clear, the Code gives a basis for a complaint to the labour authorities.

## Maternity benefit and crèche

Maternity benefit now sits in Chapter VI of the Code on Social Security, which replaced the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961. The substance builds on the 2017 amendment, which raised paid maternity leave from 12 weeks to 26 weeks for a woman with fewer than two surviving children, with up to eight weeks allowed before the expected delivery. A woman with two or more surviving children receives a shorter period, up to 12 weeks. To qualify, a woman must have worked a minimum of 80 days in the twelve months before the expected delivery. The chapter applies to factories, mines, plantations and government establishments, as well as to shops and establishments with ten or more employees.

The same legal framework requires a crèche in establishments with 50 or more employees. For a mother returning to work, the availability of a safe place for a small child is often the difference between staying in the job and leaving it. The detail of how crèche facilities are to be provided, shared or paid for is left to rules, so the practical value of this provision will depend on those rules.

## Night work and safety

Allowing women to work at night, with consent and with safety arrangements, opens up sectors such as manufacturing, services and logistics where shifts run around the clock. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code states that women may be employed in all establishments for all types of work, and where hazardous operations are involved the Government may require the employer to put adequate safeguards in place first. The condition of consent is important, since a right to work at night should not become a compulsion.

The harder questions are on the ground: transport to and from the workplace, lighting and security at the premises, and complaint mechanisms that women actually trust. The Code's requirement that grievance committees have women's representation is an attempt at the last of these.

## The numbers that matter: who is outside the Codes' reach

The most honest assessment is that the provisions above mostly help women in formal employment. Most working women, however, are in the informal sector, in farm work, small trade, home-based production and domestic work, where there is often no appointment letter, no pay slip and no identifiable employer to hold to account. For them, maternity benefit and equal pay are, in practice, rarely enforced. The Code on Social Security provides for the registration of unorganised, gig and platform workers and for schemes to be funded by governments and, in the case of platform work, by aggregators, who contribute 1 to 2 per cent of annual turnover, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay to workers. Registration is the first step to any benefit, so how quickly and accessibly it is done will decide whether women in these jobs are helped.

## What is still missing

- **Domestic workers** do not yet have a central law of their own that sets wages, hours and rest for them as a group.
- **Safety at the workplace and on the way to it**, especially for night shifts, needs rules that are specific and enforced.
- **Unpaid care work**, which many women do in addition to paid work, is not recognised in labour law or social security.
- **Scheme workers**, most of them women, are called honorary workers and are outside the Codes' protections for employees. In a written reply to the Lok Sabha on 1 August 2025, the Government said it had no proposal to raise the honorarium of Anganwadi workers and helpers, which was Rs 4,500 a month for workers at regular centres and Rs 2,250 for helpers, as last revised in October 2018.

## What BMS says

BMS has said that welfare for women workers must begin with registration and recognition. In the BMS family, the Anganwadi, ASHA and mid-day meal federations are largely organisations of women, and their demands, from a higher honorarium to a pension and eventual regularisation, are in substance demands for women's economic dignity. In its memorandum to the Labour Minister on 21 November 2025, BMS asked for higher honoraria for Anganwadi workers and helpers, ASHA workers, mid-day meal workers and other scheme-based workers, and for the regularisation of long-term contract workers. These are demands that the Codes do not meet on their own and that call for budget decisions.

## Closing thought

The Codes state some good principles for women: equal pay, non-discrimination, maternity cover, a crèche, a voice on grievance committees. Whether a woman in a village anganwadi, a city home or a field gets any of this depends on being counted. The task for 2026 is therefore not to repeat that the law exists but to see that registration, rules and funding reach the woman who is working without a letter, a slip or a contract. A society's labour law can be judged by how it treats those who work the hardest for the least recognition.
